title: China’s Batanes presence tests regional peace pledge

blocks.text: While China’s stated commitment to completing the Code of Conduct (COC) on the South China Sea is significant in promoting regional stability, a defense analyst reminded Beijing that “intentions don’t build trust, actions do.”

Chester Cabalza, president of the think tank International Development and Security Cooperation, made the statement as China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) expressed their commitment to reaching a consensus on the COC.

The Philippines, which chaired the Asean Summit this year, had pushed for a legally binding agreement that would establish clear rules of conduct in the South China Sea to prevent maritime incidents from escalating into armed confrontations.

But as the summit ended, the draft remained 80% complete, the Department of Foreign Affairs said, pointing to unresolved debates over its legally binding nature, geographic scope and the 2016 arbitral award as reasons Manila was unable to seal the deal.

Still, Marcos commended China and Asean member states for reaffirming their commitment to sustaining earlier efforts to complete the long-delayed code, which could help minimize tensions in the South China Sea between Beijing and other claimants.
Inconsistent

Cabalza, however, told the Inquirer that if China wants a credible COC, “there must be restraint at sea and not just promises at the negotiating table,” because “confidence comes from what happens in the water.”

His comment came more than a month after the Philippine Coast Guard drove away a Chinese research vessel off Batanes after it stayed for four days in an area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.
The encounter happened almost three months after Chinese scholars and commentators claimed that Batanes once belonged to China through Taiwan, a claim the Philippines dismissed as baseless.

In July, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) confirmed that Chinese research vessels had periodically traversed waters off Batanes through “illegal tracks” and that the government had challenged Chinese research vessels over the past few years.

“Long before this false claim came out, the AFP had already heightened its posture all over the country with an outward-looking posture,” Trinidad said in a statement delivered at Camp Aguinaldo in Quezon City in response to the presence of Chinese vessels in Batanes.
For Cabalza, “sincerity is proven in the open sea.”
He said China should back its diplomatic intentions with concrete confidence-building measures, especially since China itself has called on Asean to promote peace and mutual trust.
Gateway

As for the claim that Batanes was “legally part” of Taiwan, Stratbase Institute President Victor Andres Manhit described its repetition as a “clear attempt to manufacture ambiguity where none exists.”
Cabalza explained in an interview that Batanes is the lock on the First Island Chain and that “whoever holds these islands controls the gateway between the South China Sea and the open Pacific.”

“Closer to Taipei than Manila, Batanes has transformed from a quiet northern outpost into the frontline of regional deterrence,” he said, pointing to the need to protect Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost province.
“To safeguard Batanes, we must pair stronger local maritime presence with ironclad alliances, turning our northern frontier from a vulnerable target into an unshakeable shield,” he said.

China’s desire to control Taiwan is inseparable from its wider objective of dominating the First Island Chain — a maritime containment line stretching from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines toward Borneo.
From Beijing’s perspective, the First Island Chain functions as both a defensive perimeter and a constraining barrier between China’s “near seas” and the open Pacific.

Control of the chain would strengthen China’s ability to project naval power while increasing pressure on key trade routes and intensifying security risks for countries that sit along or rely on the corridor. /dm
